There are 149 citation entries in total, and 109 materials after deduplication: different conclusions from the same paper each occupy one entry, because different original passages are cited. All entries were run through verify_sources.ts: arXiv entries were checked by id against the official API for the real title (all 70 matched), web entries were checked that the page is accessible and the citation exists verbatim (two of the Notion pages are front-end rendered; they were verified after rendering with a browser).

gaps.text: No public material was found that gives an empirical threshold for “how many times a single-point spike in gradient norm counts as anomalous”; our “pro step 19 6× is a single-step anomaly” is still a self-defined multiple, and the public literature only states that spikes bring instability (2502.17055) and provides a mechanism (2509.02479), with no comparable multiple baseline.

No public material was found that gives the typical magnitude or healthy range of “truncation ratio” metrics such as actor/pg_tis_clipfrac in real large-scale RL runs; therefore, whether the local 1e-4 magnitude is on the healthy side or the high side cannot be compared against a public baseline.

No public case was found that directly discusses “entropy monotonically rising within a few dozen steps while avg@n also rises”: entropy-mechanism(2505.22617) describes the opposite direction, and DAPO only treats “avoiding entropy collapse” as a means; therefore, the claim that “entropy rising in this run is benign” lacks positive supporting evidence, and only boundary conditions were found (DISPO says excess will degrade).

No public material was found explaining “why pg_clipfrac and ppo_kl would both be identically zero at the same time, rather than the entire tag being missing”. The verl documentation only gives the definitions of the two, without discussing the interpretation of this phenomenon; our explanation is self-consistent reasoning, not an official line.

No public material was found that separately discusses entropy split by harness (grouped readings such as actor/agentic/entropy_loss and actor/code/entropy_loss), i.e., “whether grouped entropy should be treated as the same physical quantity” has no counterpart in public work.

In the briefing's reference starting points, the titles of the two ids 2506.17863 (labeled The Art of Scaling RL Compute) and 2506.10947 (labeled Pass@k Training) both do not match, and I was unable to locate the corresponding papers with the correct titles (the two respectively belong to groups D/C and were not further verified in this group).

No public material explains this dashboard's own tag conventions: how exactly k in partial/<k> is counted (pro opens only 8 buckets, flash opens 10), why Σ_k n_tokens_k is only 44%~56% of perf/total_num_tokens at the same step, and the denominator relationship between the two slices partial/agentic and partial/<category>/<dataset> (the sum of the two exceeds 1.6×).

The train_infer_diff/new_infer/F(tau=*) family has no metric with the same name or definition in the public literature, and no material specifies the unit of tau; verl only has rollout_is_ratio_fraction_high (fraction of IS weights above threshold) and log_ppl_abs_diff (mean absolute log-perplexity difference), two names that are close but have different definitions.

No public statement was found for the shift-share identity 「global KL exactly equals Σ_k frac_k × KL_k」 (our verification correlation is 1.000000); public material only separates the 「engine difference term」 and the 「staleness term」 at the conceptual level (arXiv:2605.12070, verl Rollout Correction), without giving a convention for weighted summation by freshness bucket.

No public practice or threshold reference was found for splitting staleness by dataset, so there is no public baseline to compare against for partial/code/dataset-yfch/avg_staleness being as high as 7.27.

「asymmetric importance sampling」 as a named method has no corresponding literature in a search of the entire arXiv corpus; the closest is Asymmetric REINFORCE (reinterpreted by arXiv:2509.24203 as a regularized form of REINFORCE), and no material supports the 「splitting into four-sided clipping by positive/negative advantage or by high/low boundaries」 convention.

No public material was found discussing the definition of the agentic data slice; agentic is also not among the categories declared by this dashboard's meta.json, so it is impossible to use public material to explain the phenomenon that partial/agentic/avg_staleness has a global correlation of 0.9999.

No public method was found that does this processing: 「split by advantage sign → withdraw part of the positive-advantage mass → add mass to negative advantages → then rescale each sign's total back to its original value」. In arXiv searches, "advantage clipping" and "positive and negative advantages" scaling both returned 0 hits; the 4 papers hit by "asymmetric clipping" (e.g., VEPO, Entropy-Preserving RL) are work in the entropy/constraint direction, unrelated to this site's penalty/signed/* mechanism.

No public material was found that discusses or implements 「within-sign total conservation」: the form in which train/adv_pos_sum_post_penalty and pre are exactly equal pointwise has no counterpart in public methods (GRPO's within-group division by std normalization instead changes the total).

No public literature was found that names avg@n (the average over problems of the per-problem success proportion across n attempts, n=16) as an independent metric. HumanEval only gives the unbiased estimator definition of pass@k; passrate/one, passrate/zero, and the three-way decomposition avg@n = one + middle-bucket proportion × middle-bucket mass are this telemetry's own convention.

Could not obtain the verbatim original text of Section 3.1 of the Dr. GRPO main text regarding the 「direction」 of the std normalization bias: both arXiv HTML fetches were truncated before entering that section, and ar5iv does not have this paper; only the Figure 1 caption and abstract-level wording were excerpted (「removing the length and std normalization terms」).

No public material was found that defines dynsam/infra_error/seq_rate, this kind of 「proportion of detected infra failure sequences」: public work discusses rollout failures and resampling, but there is no definition or convention for this specific ratio.

No public source was found that explains why critic/rewards/min stays near −0.8 long-term; public RLVR (DAPO, etc.) uses binary {1, −1} rule rewards, and a floor score like −0.8 belongs to this site's private grading convention.

No quantitative public discussion was found on this specific direction, 「the systematic bias of within-group std normalization against low-variance prompts」 (only Dr. GRPO's qualitative claim and the counterargument of 2601.23135).

The pre-grading route discard (routed/off accounts for about 48.9% of groups_total) cannot be found in any public material: no paper or documentation describes the design of 「first excluding half of the candidate groups from grading by routing」, and there is no convention to compare against. The closest thing in public literature is DAPO's dynamic sampling (after oversampling, filter out prompts with correctness rates 1 and 0), but that filters by reward and happens after scoring, which is not the same as our pre-grading routing and cannot be conflated.

The fact that the second pass was never executed (pass2_success_rate is identically 1.0 while judge_pass2_attempts is identically 0) cannot be found in public material. BAITBENCH only uses the phrase 「two-stage judge pipeline」 and does not give success rate/attempt count conventions for any stage; nor does any material discuss this kind of reading trap where 「grading is done twice but the second pass was never enabled」.

Grading takes about 570 seconds/group, with 97% spent on the first pass: no public baseline, percentile, or cost statistic was found for the per-group duration of a grader/verifier, so the 550-second order of magnitude cannot be compared with public systems, nor can the reasonableness of the 「97% in the first pass」 split be verified.

No public implementation or grading criteria can be found for the grader itself (select_v4 / select_v4_nogold); no public material can confirm whether probe in select_probe_disagree_rate specifically refers to multiple samples from the same model, different prompts, or different models.

No dedicated literature was found for “judge saturation”: an arXiv full-text search for "judge saturation" returns only 1 result, which is unrelated to the topic (customer service churn explanation), so our reading of “judge saturation” has no provenance.

There is no public material for the rubric tier definitions and ordering direction of select_tier_share_T1/T2/T3/H (which tier is harder, whether H is hard or hold); MiMo-7B only mentions test-difficulty-driven code-reward, without rubric tier naming.

No citable paper was found for the compute-performance scaling law of RL training (whether performance can be predicted from compute): the 2506.17863 given in the briefing is actually another paper (see notes), and consecutive searches of the arXiv search API in this session were also rejected multiple times. perf/total_num_tokens is currently only tied to qualitative statements from MiMo official such as “efficiently scaling RL compute” and MiMo-VL’s compute scale descriptions, which is context rather than scaling-law evidence.

There is no public material for the criteria of env/possible_leak (what counts as a leak, whether the statistical window is instantaneous or cumulative); 2609.02246 describes leak patterns such as an agent reading cached answer keys from the environment, but does not give a corresponding metric definition.

Public baselines for sandbox turnover rate/environment error rate: MiMo official only gave “10,000+ concurrent pods and 70% environment setup success rate”, without giving the denominator criteria for sandbox lifecycle, turnover count, or error rate; therefore our “both runs’ sandbox turnover is around 14x” can only be considered self-attested and cannot be compared with official or third-party sources.
No public material directly argues for the causality between grading time and data staleness (slow grading → partial/avg_staleness increases); this is an inference from this telemetry.

No public material was found that gives the official definitions for the judged / in flight columns in the mimo.xiaomi.com/rl sampler table. The only things that can be confirmed are: the English labels of these two columns come from the original site’s own rendering code; the judged column is reported only on a subset of code data sources and is always no greater than accepted; the per-source sum of the in flight column is always equal to remain + remain_partial on the dashboard. Their exact counting unit (tasks or sequences, whether partial rollout is included) is not publicly explained.

The calculations on this site are all “relationships internal to the data”; they can prove definitions and identities, but cannot prove that a certain reading is methodologically optimal —— that layer can only rely on public literature.
pro step 19 is the last step within the recorded range, so it cannot be verified whether the gradient spike will become the new normal.

r3：【Key conclusion: Is there a public counterpart for penalty/signed/*?】No. In public methods, the “asymmetric” treatment of positive/negative advantages all acts on the importance sampling ratio or the surrogate objective, not on the mass allocation of advantage: DAPO's Clip-Higher merely splits the upper and lower clipping bounds and loosens the upper bound (explicitly keeping εlow unchanged, on the grounds that increasing it would push token probabilities toward 0); dual-clip PPO only adds a lower bound c·Â_t to the objective when Â_t<0; what it clips is an excessively large negative update. Neither changes the distribution of advantage, and neither has the step of “replenishing mass and then renormalizing back to the original total according to sign”.
